q: Two hold a garment; each says, 'I found it, all of it is mine.' What is the ruling?
options: Each swears he owns no less than half, and they divide
The one holding it more firmly takes it
It stays in court until Eliyahu comes
They divide without an oath
why: Both are in possession, so they split it, each swearing to the half he receives.

q: Why does each swear 'no less than half' rather than 'all of it is mine'?
options: 'All' would force one of them into a false oath; 'half' would make him give up his claim
Because the court awards only half
Because an oath on a whole object is forbidden
Because a half is easier to prove
why: The formula avoids a certain false oath and still matches the ruling exactly.

q: One says 'all of it is mine' and the other 'half of it is mine.' How do they divide?
options: ¾ and ¼, each swearing accordingly
½ and ½
All to the one who claims all
⅔ and ⅓
why: Half is conceded to the first, so only the other half is in dispute, and it is split.

q: When do they divide without any oath?
options: When they admit each other's claims, or each has witnesses
When the item is worth less than a *perutah*
When it is an animal
Never
why: An oath is imposed only where there is no other way to establish the claims.

q: What does 'all of it is mine', added to 'I found it', teach on the compound reading?
options: Seeing a found item does not acquire it
A finder must announce it
A purchase is stronger than a find
Both must swear twice
why: In everyday speech 'I found it' can mean 'I saw it'; the addition shows sight alone doesn't acquire.

An oath taken in vain
Property of uncertain ownership
A certain claim
why: "He is losing nothing" — the oath targets the person who rationalizes, not the brazen thief.

q: Why can the Mishnah follow Ben Nannas, who objects to an oath where one side must be lying?
options: Both may have lifted it together, so both may swear truly
Ben Nannas allows false oaths for property
Only one of them swears
Ben Nannas wasn't speaking of found items
why: Each may really own half, so no *shevuat shav* is certain here.

q: What is Sumakhos's rule for property of uncertain ownership (*mamon ha'mutal be'safek*)?
options: They divide it
The claimant must bring proof
The one in possession swears and keeps it
It is left until Eliyahu comes
why: For example, a calf found beside a sold cow. The Rabbis put the burden of proof on the claimant.
